title: Choosing potato varieties
subtitle: Earlies, maincrops, and the flavour-versus-storage trade-off
excerpt: UK potato varieties are grouped as first early, second early, and maincrop. The choice depends on when you want to eat them, how much storage space you have, and whether you are growing in a container or a border. Blight resistance is a consideration for maincrops in wetter parts of the country.
sourceNotes: RHS potato variety guide (rhs.org.uk). USDA cooperative extension notes on potato variety selection, public domain. Historical variety records from UK Recommended List, public domain.

glossaryTerms.definition: Waxy varieties have a firm, moist, salad-type texture and hold their shape when boiled. Floury varieties have a dry, starchy texture and fall apart easily, making them ideal for mashing, roasting, and baking. Most first early varieties are waxy; maincrops range from waxy (Desiree) to highly floury (King Edward, Maris Piper, Rooster).

content.text: Choosing by season type and texture first, then variety, narrows the selection quickly. First earlies give early summer new potatoes for immediate eating; maincrops give a storable bulk harvest in autumn. The
distinction determines whether a variety suits your kitchen.

Planted late February to early April; harvested June to July. Arran Pilot: traditional, waxy, good flavour, widely available. Rocket: very early, good yields, firm flesh. Swift: one of the earliest of all, suited to containers and smaller plots. Casablanca: excellent waxy flavour, widely recommended for new potato eating.

Planted March to April; harvested July to August. Charlotte: the most popular second early, waxy, good flavour, widely grown for salads. Nicola: waxy, yellow flesh, reliable. Kestrel: versatile, good all-rounder, some resistance to common scab.

Planted April to May; harvested September to October. Maris Piper: the most widely grown UK maincrop, floury, excellent for chips and mash, good yields. Desiree: red-skinned, versatile, less floury than Maris Piper, some drought tolerance. King Edward: traditional, highly floury, excellent roasting potato, lower disease resistance. Sarpo Mira and Sarpo Axona: high blight resistance, good choice for wetter areas and organic growers.

For containers, first and second early varieties are best: they need no earthing up in deep bags, finish quickly, and are picked young when the flavour is at its best. Charlotte, Swift, Casablanca, and International Kidney (the Jersey Royal parent) all grow well in a 35 litre planting sack.
